newsitem.title: UK: British astronomers devastated at rocket failure.
newsitem.headline: British astronomers devastated at rocket failure.

text.p: British astronomers expressed dismay on Sunday at the news that Russia's Mars-96 mission had failed just after lift-off and was likely to burn up in the Earth's atmosphere.
Several British experiments were aboard the doomed probe, the second space mission to fail this year.
Last Spring, British scientists watched in horror as the European Space Agency's Ariane 5 exploded with millions of pounds (dollars) worth of their experiments aboard.

Russia's $64 million rocket failed to break out of the Earth's orbit on Saturday and most of it was expected to fall back and burn up on re-entry into the atmosphere. It had been due to reach Mars on September 12 next year.
"We lost 10 years of work just like that," said David Southwood of Imperial College London. "It's a tremendous blow to us. I don't know what could come out of the ashes of Mars-96."
One instrument aboard Mars-96 was put together by the Mullard Space Science Laboratory near Guildford in southern England.
Known as Fonema, it was meant to measure changes in the atmosphere of the red planet. Such details will help scientists determine if there was, or could be, life on Mars.
"We are particularly disappointed about this one for three reasons," said Andrew Coates, one of the project's directors.
"First of all the science that we were going to get from it was excellent. It would have told us how quickly the atmosphere was being lost.
"Second, the instrument design was particularly innovative and very competitive in world terms.
"And third it comes on heels of Cluster and Ariane 5. It comes as a very big blow to our group."
Coates said he could not blame the Russian scientists. "We are sure that they did their very best to test it as well as they could but sometimes there just isn't the time."

Geraint Jones, a research scientist who helped design and build the project, said he and colleagues had been spared having to watch the disaster on live television as they had the Ariane explosion. But they had watched regular updates by computer, on the Internet's World Wide Web.

"It's been a double blow to us. Ideally we'd like to fly the instruments again but it's fairly unlikely to be on a Russian one," Jones said. He noted that Russian scientists, short of funding, had worked without pay just to get the mission launched.
He said it would be a long time before the efforts could be duplicated. "Launch opportunities to Mars only come round every two years. We have to wait."
He added: "It's just annoying when these failures occur not through any fault of our own. It looked as though our instruments would have operated perfectly. It's frustrating."
Coates said British scientists were trying to persuade the European Space Agency to have a second try at the Cluster mission which blew up with Ariane 5.
Mars-96 was the second of three planned trips from Earth to Mars this autumn. The United States launched a robot mission two weeks ago and a second mission will blast off on December 2.
